work.title: SERVICE ECONOMICS
work.subtitle: A demand-capacity and unit-model workbook
work.scope: A fictional Review Sessions capacity model. Minutes and teaching credits are illustrative; credits are not currency, prices, revenue or profit, and no actual service, staffing or demand is supplied.

pages.title: Define one service unit before doing arithmetic.
pages.lead: The fictional service unit is one bounded document-review session lasting forty-five teaching minutes. It examines a passage and its source question, not the correctness of every claim in a document.
pages.body: Specify what is included and what remains outside the unit. This workbook establishes no operating service, professional verification, appointment availability or commercial contract. A real service definition needs appropriate responsibility and scope.
pages.detail: The model uses one arbitrary planning window. Neither the duration nor the resource assumptions are validated observations of actual work.
pages.question: What must be clear before a request can count as one service unit?

records.label: Unit
records.prompt: One bounded review of a passage and source question.

records.label: Duration assumption
records.prompt: 45 teaching minutes per completed session.

records.label: Exclusion
records.prompt: No guarantee of correctness or full-document approval.

pages.title: Keep demand assumptions separate from bookings.
pages.lead: The three model demand cases contain six, eight and ten requested sessions. They are authored planning inputs, not a waiting list, booked work or a measure of customer interest.
pages.body: An actual demand assessment would need a defined request, a relevant window and an appropriate source. Counting enquiries as completed work would conceal both uncertainty and the delivery constraint.
pages.detail: Demand above the model’s capacity produces an unmet count, not automatic permission to shorten sessions or make commitments.
pages.question: Which definition would distinguish a request from a confirmed suitable booking?

records.label: Lower case
records.prompt: 6 hypothetical requests.

records.label: Reference case
records.prompt: 8 hypothetical requests.

records.label: Higher case
records.prompt: 10 hypothetical requests, not actual bookings.

pages.title: Derive capacity from the stated time assumptions.
pages.lead: The model starts with four hundred and fifty available teaching minutes and reserves ninety. That leaves three hundred and sixty minutes for the defined service units.
pages.body: At forty-five minutes each, floor of 360 divided by 45 gives eight sessions. The reserve is a modelling boundary, not spare time that the workbook authorises someone to consume. No actual staffing arrangement is supplied.
pages.detail: Changing a unit’s duration or the reserve changes the model. Preserve the original assumption and examine whether the service scope would still be appropriate.
pages.question: Which assumption must be checked before calling eight sessions feasible?

records.label: Available / reserve
records.prompt: 450 minutes less 90 reserved = 360.

records.label: Unit / capacity
records.prompt: 360 ÷ 45 = 8 whole sessions.

records.label: Feasibility boundary
records.prompt: No observed duration, staff availability or workload approval.

pages.title: Map the work around the session.
pages.lead: Before a session, clarify the passage and relevant source. During it, inspect the stated question. After it, retain an appropriately agreed note about what remains unresolved.
pages.body: The time model does not separately measure preparation, coordination or follow-up. If those activities draw on the same available minutes, the capacity calculation must be revised rather than quietly treating them as free.
pages.detail: The ninety-minute reserve is not an itemised estimate of all supporting work. Real delivery needs a more complete account of tasks and responsibilities.
pages.question: Which supporting task could make the simple capacity assumption misleading?

records.label: Before
records.prompt: Clarify scope and source availability.

records.label: During
records.prompt: Review the bounded passage-question relationship.

records.label: After
records.prompt: Record the remaining question under an appropriate agreement.

pages.title: Use a unit model without pretending it is money.
pages.lead: Each completed session receives ten benefit credits and uses four variable resource credits. The unit contribution is six credits; fixed resources are twenty credits per teaching window.
pages.body: Credits are arbitrary non-monetary quantities used to illustrate structure. Net credits equal six times completed sessions minus twenty. They are not prices, sales, wages, cash flow or profit.
pages.detail: The smallest whole number covering the model’s fixed credits is ceiling of 20 divided by 6, which is four completed sessions. This is a teaching threshold, not a real financial break-even.
pages.question: What evidence would be needed before constructing an actual commercial unit model?

records.label: Unit contribution
records.prompt: 10 − 4 = 6 teaching credits.

records.label: Window net
records.prompt: 6 × completed sessions − 20 fixed credits.

records.label: Teaching threshold
records.prompt: ceil(20 ÷ 6) = 4 sessions; not financial break-even.

pages.title: Distinguish fixed assumptions from fixed obligations.
pages.lead: The model holds twenty fixed credits and a ninety-minute reserve unchanged across the three cases. That is a comparison choice, not evidence of an actual obligation or a complete operating cost base.
pages.body: A real service may have resources that change in steps, shared capacity or commitments outside the planning window. Identify those conditions before translating a simple unit model into a decision.
pages.detail: There are no rent, salary, tax, technology or insurance figures in this workbook. Do not interpret the teaching total as an actual cost estimate.
pages.question: Which supposedly fixed resource might change when the delivery arrangement changes?

records.label: Model assumption
records.prompt: 20 fixed teaching credits per window.

records.label: Time boundary
records.prompt: 90 minutes reserved in the capacity model.

records.label: Missing costs
records.prompt: No actual spending, rates or contractual obligations supplied.

pages.title: Compare the three demand cases.
pages.lead: Demand six, eight and ten produces delivery six, eight and eight under the capacity ceiling. Unmet counts are zero, zero and two. Unused service minutes are ninety, zero and zero.
pages.body: Net teaching credits are sixteen, twenty-eight and twenty-eight. The higher demand case cannot raise delivery or net credits without changing another assumption. No actual utilisation or financial performance is reported.
pages.detail: Service minutes are delivered sessions times forty-five. Unused service minutes exclude the ninety-minute reserve, which remains separate in every case.
pages.question: Which total stops changing when the capacity ceiling is reached?

records.label: Lower case
records.prompt: 6 delivered; 90 unused service minutes; net 16.

records.label: Reference case
records.prompt: 8 delivered; 0 unused service minutes; net 28.

records.label: Higher case
records.prompt: 8 delivered; 2 unmet requests; net remains 28.

pages.title: Treat quality as a condition, not an automatic output.
pages.lead: Completing eight units in the model says nothing about the suitability or quality of an actual review. A capacity equation cannot establish whether a participant had enough context or support.
pages.body: Do not shorten a session merely to make the arithmetic fit more requests. Consider task complexity, access arrangements and the agreed review boundary before changing the unit definition or reserve.
pages.detail: The workbook provides no quality score, satisfaction result or validated duration. Any real trade-off requires relevant information and appropriate responsibility.
pages.question: What could be lost if the unit were compressed without changing its scope?

records.label: Scope check
records.prompt: The task remains bounded and understandable.

records.label: Support check
records.prompt: Relevant access and review conditions are considered.

records.label: Evidence gap
records.prompt: No actual service-quality or duration observations supplied.

pages.title: Build a validation checklist around the unknowns.
pages.lead: Before using a similar model, examine the request definition, actual task duration, supporting work, appropriate reserve and commercial conditions. Each needs a source rather than a confident guess.
pages.body: Validate the meaning of the unit before seeking a precise number. A carefully calculated result can still be irrelevant if the service scope or planning window has changed.
pages.detail: Start with scope and responsibility, then inspect time and demand information. Only use actual financial inputs when they are available and appropriately defined.
pages.question: Which unknown would most change the interpretation of the model?

records.label: Scope evidence
records.prompt: An agreed definition of the service and exclusions.

records.label: Time evidence
records.prompt: Appropriate observations of the full task, not just contact time.

records.label: Commercial evidence
records.prompt: Actual terms and costs; none supplied here.

pages.title: Turn the workbook into operating questions.
pages.lead: The useful questions are whether the unit is meaningful, whether the time boundary is defensible and what happens when suitable requests exceed capacity. The point model cannot answer those questions alone.
pages.body: This document remains a fictional planning example. No actual service, pricing decision, staffing approval or profitability claim follows from its calculations. Record which source would be needed for a more consequential decision.
pages.detail: Carry forward one uncertainty about scope, one about resources and one about demand. Keep the teaching calculation available for inspection without upgrading it into a forecast.
pages.question: What should be learned before the service concept is developed further?

records.label: Scope question
records.prompt: What work is included and appropriately supported?

records.label: Resource question
records.prompt: What actually constrains delivery in the relevant setting?

records.label: Demand question
records.prompt: Which requests represent a suitable, defined need?
